items.body:
​Jake Muir back on enmossed with an album of "all goop’d up ambient bits from black and death metal records..."

Stirring together and re-seasoning the stickiest bits of his favorite metal records, Jake Muir dreams up an atmospheric, bathhouse-ready reaction to the most extreme soundscapes, enhancing lysergic moments to bring out parallels with gear from Coil, :zoviet*france:, Pinkcourtesyphone, Main or even Ulver.

What makes music heavy, exactly? Is it simply the volume itself, or could it be the spread of culturally assured elements that make our skin prickle and our ears focus in on fight or flight terrors like animalistic cries, rattling chains or grim liturgical chants? Muir has been fascinated with rock music since he was a kid, poring over byzantine, maximal offerings from bands like Meshuggah and Nine Inch Nails. And it's an obsession that's led him through the bullrushes of death and black metal, genres that often veer into experimental territory, crossing the streams with industrial, noise and of course dark ambient. 'Pareidolia' is Muir's celebration of bleak metal's nightmarish atmospheres, sounds that make the blast beats, hoarse vocals and smudgy chords sound even more substantial without technically being loud. 

Pulled away from their context, these textures are compellingly theatrical: whooshing ice winds, creaking branches, scraping metal, chiming bells, plucked strings and heaving drones. They're sounds that situate us in death and black metal's ancestral Northern homeland, in some remote cabin hemmed in by harsh weather and prowling wolves. So heard on their own, it's predictable that we end up trudging similarly cinematic territory as the "dark ambient" forebears like Lustmord and Deathprod or more recent exponents Svarte Greiner and Lussuria. Muir's idea for the album was a little different; spurred on by his back-and-forth with Even Caminiti on 2022's ace 'Talisman' album, he attempted to use these bleak fantasies to power the kind of heady, sexually-charged moods that goosebump'd thru his breakout 'Bathhouse Blues' without losing the folk horror cogitation of last year's sacred meditation 'Campana Sonans'.

In fact, 'Pareidolia' is supposed to play like an illusion - even the name of the album is a reference to this. Muir wants to rope us in with familiarity before waltzing us through a parallel history of isolationist, industrial ambient gear, the kind of guitar-muddling, metal-aware grot that linked Nocturnal Emissions and Z'EV and Robert Hampson's electroacoustic rock duo Main with heady set texts from Eno, Daniel Lanois, Stuart Dempster and Steve Roach. The album isn't just a DJ set of the quiet moments from recent RYM metal side-quests, as you'll hear as soon as you plug into opener 'Beithir'. Between the blustery soundscapes and knife-sharpening SFX, there's a melodic pulse and echoing oscillations that wouldn't sound out of place on an IASOS record, while the dense, Sunn O)))-adjacent bass drone takes on a surprisingly humid character, winding itself around weightless pads and spirit breaths.

On 'Unholy Apparitions' meanwhile, Muir's phantasmagorical scratches and chirps are re-fashioned into brain-tickling ASMR purrs that surf across white noise clouds and low end rumbles, while on  'Cathedral of Decay', environments that sound as if they've been recorded in a damp crypt are shifted to the sauna, each minor key flourish transformed into a furtive glance to the side. It's the air that's heavy, not the music itself.

items.body:
Peak Oil sublabel FO returns with a strong debut of late night, air-fried trip hop from Cold Light, flocking like moths to an illbient flame tipped FFO Jabu, Tricky, Sleepdial, Shell Company, Space Afrika.

Cold Light are Bristol’s Birthmark & Withdrawn, Portland’s Best Available Technology, Rael & Eldon out of London, and Hungarian CSNL. Some half a decade after a ‘Live at the Laundromat’ tape introduction, the collective unveil ‘Coldtron 2’, a sparingly sensuous slant on the lush pastures between trip hop, smoked-out dub soul and illbient jazz, inflected with the voices of Elaine Malone, Akeko and British-Nigerian sound designer Tony Onuchukwu. With remarkable restraint - especially considering so many hands are on board - they keep everything pared-back to creaking, atmospheric fundamentals for 40 minutes of smouldering storytelling, passing the torch across chapters of zoot-end poetic monologues, from stylised rap to spoken word, in a spectrum of accents speaking to the group’s far flung coordinates. 

Call it downbeat neo-noir or trip hop 2.0, the sound is clearly in thrall to the ‘90s OGs - Tricky, Portishead, Massive Attack - yet gauzily distinguished from its forebears by the production’s pall of dematerialised textures and an enervated feel for screwed subs and glimmers of sounds that emerged in trip hop’s fall-out. The Bristol night air is thick with sferic crackle and diffused sax in ’Smoke Signal’ thru the Memotone-esque eldritch of ‘Troposphere Test’, taking in a tacit nod to Mobb Deep via Tricky on the smouldering ‘Riot’, or even Civilistjävel!’s low-key electrodub in ‘Lean Wid It…’,    and Sleepdial’s slurred drums on ‘I’ve Known Fires’. But they’re most potent on ‘Fields in B’ with eight mins of smudged Rhythm & Sound steppas bass anchoring the bluest sax plumes and blunted bars, ideal for ashtray dreamers.

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia draws a line under over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair, T++.

An artist keenly observed since those initial anonymous gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and through a cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at the project’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence, and in effect feels like an aesthetic descendent of Torsten Pröfrock’s convulsive prototypes as T++. 

Ultimately, though, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.

items.body:
Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. Check for the uncanny frissons of ‘Lam Cheung’ and its slew of piquant percussive works, all shimmering with the type of timeless lustre we’ve come to expect from Sullivan & DINTE’s magpie picks...

"In Lao PDR, music was seemingly everywhere. Walking through an open field outside Savannakhet to the sound of someone playing a khaen on a distant porch, the bracing rush of electronic molam from of one of Vientiane’s many aging malls, the awkward blending of the blind so u player’s voice with the bustling sounds of Luang Prabang’s night market.

It was in that UNESCO World Heritage Site that I found most of the CDs and CD-Rs from which I’ve ripped the tracks for this compilation. I’m almost certain I picked up a thumb drive at the night market that held many hours of additional music that could have been included, but if so, I’ve misplaced it, lost it for good, or simply misremember purchasing it in the first place. What I do remember is that these discs were literally the last copies in the cafe, museum, bookstore, and night market where I bought them, and not all of them played all the way through without sonic deterioration.

The sounds compiled here play in stark contrast to the more contemporary recordings I found in Laos, most of which featured some form of upbeat digital workstation molam or children’s songs. In addition to the ever-present khaen, this collection includes recordings of the sanai, a single-reed instrument fashioned from a water buffalo horn, the ceremonial khong nyai gong, the pi and similar free-reeds, and at least a dozen more traditional instruments played by Lao and ethnic minority artists. While some of these tracks were laid down in Vientiane or Luang Prabang, most were recorded near where the artists lived, from the legendary Vat Phou in the far south to the former Pathet Lao capital Xam Neua in the northeast.

Unlike Laurent Jeanneau’s more focused Lao collections for Akuphone and Sublime Frequencies, which remain among my favorite albums of all time, the present cassette-only selection is literally all over the PDR map. The sequencing is entirely in response to rhythm and texture and includes recordings from the 1970s, 80s, 90s, and early aughts. This may frustrate those with more of an ethnomusicology bent, but my hope is that the listener experiences something akin to wandering for the first time through this majestic country, encountering the last copies of forgotten recordings one after another, and hearing in these remains fragments of the past and a living musical landscape."

–Gary Sullivan (Bodega Pop)”

items.body:
The incomparable Winos dial-up a near-future fraught with glitching techno x surrealist folk artefacts supposed by mainman Morgan Buckley and his pal Ben Donohoe, a 12-track guess-again sprawl ranging from Arthur Russell-esque mood music to screwed Aphex jams.

Under the auspices of “Sworx”, an omniscient dialup modem, they parse coded waveforms in a discrete filing system, combing and recombining its data in a dozen buzzing post-techno chimeras and itchy electro jams. It’s instant classic Wah Wah Wino, freakishly playful and exerting odd sidespins on familiar styles and patterns with a ludic moxie that makes all their music so appealing.

The ‘Sworx’ system speaks its piece in a unique voice of detuned twangs and ululating electronic rhythms, shifting mercurial from what sounds like The Necks doing electro with a prepared piano on ‘OpportuniXt’, to a standout electro zinger with early AFXian vocaloids on ‘The System Works’, and Plone-esque key clatter on ‘dxmmy. pxtsy. rolodex’, thru a centrepiece calling to mind Oval’s most sublime on ‘breathwx (half_life)’. 

‘Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]’ projects an unusually optimist vision of futurism, less techno dread, more cyber-pastoral, and the trip continues to wend from displaced, outernational folk in ‘Langley Prayer Room 9’, to a masterstroke of pitchbent club sauce in ‘sWORxism_noclocks_notimekept’ that tickles rarest pleasure centres with its piquant wrong-notes and gooey groove.

Collect them all!

items.body:
After marinading in the archive for 30 years, Regis unleashes a spicy batch of hypnotic meat motors hailing from an early crest of his powers, available for the first time.

It’s no real secret that Karl O’Connor dispensed dozens of 12”s in the late ‘90s under pseudonyms that are still coming to light. Since 2003, when his energies were more focussed on the BMB duo with Surgeon, he’s really pushed the techno framework into fascinating new shapes. But, like legion others, we’re all still here for his signature early brand of girder-strength bangers, as spotted ‘In Plain Sight’ here.

The title tune plays to his classic style of white knuckle tension and kinky canter with a discordant, panic-raising lead and warehouse-ready pound, whilst an early, EBM-tooled zinger ‘We Said No’ appears via two unreleased versions; a nastier alt. 1 galvanisation, and an August 1996 mix kitted with a rictus hi-hat backbone. 

Finally he dispenses an August 1996 mix of ‘Backwards Man’, which doesn’t appear on the EP of the same name nor on ‘Hard Eduction 1931’ sets, and fully endures on modern floors for its mind-bending, pitching lead and dead slinky, brutalist gait.

items.body:
Pushing back against "Acid Nostalgia", Lawrence English dreams of a moonlit future on 'The Rest is My Ghost', bringing in assistance from a heap of collaborators, including members of The Necks, Swans, Mats Gustafsson, Rully Shabara and Lena Ito for a strong set that’s more curdled than harmonious, and all the better for it.

'The Rest is My Ghost' is more radical and political than anything we’ve heard from English in a while, more in line with 2014's charged 'Wilderness of Mirrors' and its brilliant follow-up 'Cruel Optimism’. Provoked by a conversation with Adam Curtis and driven by texts from Mark Fisher, JG Ballard, Katsuhiro Otomo, Franco Berardi, Kate Crawford and Alexie Yurchak and cultural architectural realities like the loss of Los Angeles' signature street lamps and Japan's Metabolists, English searches for a "political projection of nostalgia" that he can subsequently rupture. "Like acid poured onto a surface," he writes. "this use of nostalgia seeks to erode the complexity and texture of lived connection and longing, which has until recently guided contemplations of nostalgia."

He's talking about the difference between dreaming of your own past and being sold a neatly packaged pseudo-reality, its highs and lows smoothed over for easier consumption. To represent this concept musically, English moves away from dense distortions and instead collects up instrumental performances from a wide swathe of notable players including The Necks’ Chris Abrahams and Tony Buck, Madeleine Cocolas, Mats Gustafsson, Thor Harris, Heinz Riegler and Swans’ Norman Westberg among an all-star lineup. Perusing the personnel list and projecting your expectations on the material is part of the process and so English obscures everything purposefully, shrouding the instrumentation in reverb and gusts of hazed interference. If seeing names like pedal steel player Chuck Johnson gives you pause, that's the point. English engages in his own hauntological process, extracting the essence from the stems and imprinting it on his soundscapes. He's not eroding the material, but rather searching out the triggers that play on the imagination, inspiring futures that have never been more difficult to grasp.

And if it sounds dark, it's really not supposed to. Listen through the nocturnal hums and gentle, thrumming ambiance and you'll discover more than you bargained for - even a glimmer of hope. The result is a record that lands somewhere between classic Vangelis, Les Disques du Crépuscule's post-classical gear, Eno's fourth world experiments with John Hassell and Alan Lamb's influential sound art. In a world of drone and ambient musics that increasingly feel honed to numb the senses, this one tugs at something much deeper and more elemental.

items.body:
KAKUHAN / Sara Udon cellist Yuki Nakagawa takes a solemn yet dreamlike debut solo bow on the Unheard of Hope label - home to Mabe Fratti -  intently focussed on holistic examinations of his instrument, revealing its inner voices via various raw and processed strategies. RIYL Leila Bordreuil, Ecka Mordecai, Hildur Guðnadóttir, Okkyung Lee or Judith Hamann.

It's hard to explain just how eerily familiar Nakagawa's playing is, but you'll understand what we mean after hearing just a few moments of 'You Haze - I'. We've grown fully accustomed to the way Nakagawa handles the cello without even realizing it, absorbing his technique on records from KAKUHAN, his duo project with Koshihiro Hino, and Sara Udon alongside Naarm duo CS + Kreme. The way Nakagawa rests his bow between tones, picking up animated off-notes that make his sustained drones sound deep, dark and resonant, is genuinely personal, identifiable immediately. And although that aspect of his performance is front and center on his debut's opening track, it's the additional elements that tip us over the edge: the discreet, theremin-like wails that occupy a space just in the corner of the composition. 

After establishing his signature, Nakagawa veers away from his own convention sharply on 'CHU-MA', plucking the cello's strings and bending them as if they were attached to a koto. It's all remarkably stark at first, without much enhancement from Nakagawa's pedals and he slowly teases in different sounds that widen the instrument's range: woody creaks, knocks and growls that fill out its body and piercing overtones that go beyond the usual confines of the strings. Somehow, even using all these extended techniques, Nakagawa still manages to make music that's effortlessly enjoyable. It's bumpy, self-consciously experimental material, but not without roots - maybe best compared to Fred Frith's 'Guitar Solos' or Hans Reichel's 'The Death of the Rare Bird'.

There's even a prettiness to tracks like 'Upper and under the bridge' and 'You Haze - II' that betrays Nakagawa's resolve. But he's best when he's operating on the far fringe, turning his cello into a drum kit on the rickety, brilliant 'Grey test hits' or a vast resonator on the perplexingly huge 'Sange / Tsuki', an 8-minute xenharmonic spiral that sounds like an orchestra of fingerdrummed steel pans and a set of metal sheets being bowed in a concrete cavern. There's nothing else quite like it, we're sure of that.

items.body:
Thee most coveted collection of Coil demos surfaces on CD, opening a window onto the recording sessions for their pivotal 1991 release, ‘Love’s Secret Domain’. 

Originally collated on a demo tape for WaxTrax! records in 1989 under the working title ‘The Side Effects of Life’, these are the raw early iterations of tracks that would become ‘Love’s Secret Domain’, and arguably one of the ’90s definitive albums. Only a handful of the original cassette are known to exist, and have understandably become important artefacts in their own right, so it’s a massive buzz to finally, physically grasp the album in its entirety, here supplemented by material off the ‘Wrong Eye/Scope’ 7”.

Between the album’s two bookending versions of ‘Fidgit’, which later appeared on the ‘WaxTrax! Sampler #2’ tape in 1989, the album spools familiar yet rawer examples of Coil classics such as ‘Dark River’, ‘Teenage Lightening’ and ‘Love's Secret Domain’, each replete with haphazard fades, cuts and stereo bias, and often with lots of ferric noise. However none of that should put prospective listeners off, with results more faithful to the original than the weirdly pitched version found on YouTube and p2p sites.   

Ultimately it’s a proper find for Coil diehards, but anyone intrigued by the hidden reverse of what was going on in parallel to Rave, grunge and post rock in the phase shift between later ‘80s and early ‘90s, should fill their boots.

items.body:
15th Anniversary Remaster of Barnt’s "Geffen" via Magazine.

"Cologne-based record label Magazine celebrates the 15th anniversary of Barnt’s visionary anthem Geffen. One of electronic music's most defining tracks of the 2010s will be reissued in a 2026 remaster edition, marking the first time it receives its own dedicated standalone release.

Originally published on the legendary Cómeme imprint as part of the Various Artists EP The Power Of Now, the track rapidly became a global phenomenon. Looking back, one can hardly imagine Geffen without the 2010s, or, conversely, maybe even electronic music of that era without it. The composition mirrors the expressive possibilities of bedroom producers at the beginning of that decade—an era where artists could launch tracks into the world and have them resonate through their sheer sonic power, without major marketing efforts.

Barnt remembers: "It was one of my earliest tracks. I had just entered art school and didn't own much equipment. My MIDI keyboard only had two octaves. I would always play notes with my right hand while simultaneously shifting through the octaves with my left. This is how the hook line came to life. The production only consisted of seven or eight stems, and barely any equalizers were used during the mixdown. In hindsight, this sparse approach to production probably made it sound different and is why it hits so hard on big sound systems (while sounding unfinished to some on YouTube). At that time, we were doing a small festival on a playground in the center of Cologne. When I played the CDR there, Matias Aguayo demanded it right after. That is how it ended up on Cómeme."

The release comes with two very Magazine-esque reinterpretations from the label's two other co-founders alongside Barnt: a powerful atmospheric club remix by Jens-Uwe Beyer, and Magazine Hallucination, a wild, collaborative, psychedelic mutation by Crato and Beyer.

Jörg Burger, who already mastered the original track, is also responsible for the mastering of this release."

One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.

items.body:
Smiling C trail their Shams Dinn diamond with this bounty of Washington Go-Go picks from the short-lived Aset label’s Whax, Treo, and Latonya, all recorded and originally released c. 1986-88. Like the Shams LP, A Totally New Sound brims with pure soulful optimism and home-baked charm, but rather than early Arabic rap and ‘80s boogie, this one surveys a blindspot in most collections with some of the rarest and most special Go-Go Records in existence. 

All eight song were written by the Aset label’s in-house players, revolving song-writers Mbu Mbulu and O Jabbo, and includes their semi-released instrumental Skip, along with three beauties by the 11 year old singer Latonya which are almost worth entry alone, plus one wild one by the Whax duo, and three from Treo, the trio of Cathy Young, Delores Lidell and Linda Lawson.

Seriously, the Latonya tracks are what pop dreams are made of - precocious yet innocent, flush with colourful melodies and driven by that bustling Go-Go hustle, the super infectious Dance Time is a ready-made anthem, while Eyes Of A Child and We Will Teach The Adults weirdly also recall early ‘80s Belgian cold wave crossed with Langley Schools Music Project, or something.

The Aset Players’ Skip reveals the boogie mechanics under their pop hood, while Whax tend to the freakier side with a spot of Rick James-ian flair, and Treo’s close harmonies come out perfectly pop-wise in Demands Demands Demands, but Second Is Too Close and the forlorn romance of When Your Love Is Gone feels too weird to be pop proper, and that’s where the magick lies in this LP, between Aset’s mainstream ambition and a realness of expression that can’t be missed.

items.body:
Trane’s first album as bandleader surfaces on Craft Recordings’ guided reissue tour of classic jazz totems, spotlighting a vital period of modal jazz development from his years with the Prestige label, circa playing with Thelonious Monk and Miles Davis.

Recorded in May, 1957 and published in September that year, ’Coltrane’ marks the point when the great saxophonist began to transcend the acclaim of his peers for much wider recognition, with record sales numbers to follow suit. At the head of band including Red Garland on keys, Paul Chambers’ bass, Albert Heath on sticks, and Sahib Shihab’s baritone sax, Coltrane’s sound matures with a unique balance of smoky quintessence and modal experimentalism that would greatly inform jazz music in moving forward, outward.

That's all ideally illustrated on the daring modal suss of opener ‘Bakai’ with its switches between dervishing brass and angular rhythm to cooler stroll, and the contrast with its proceeding ‘Violets for your Furs’, and again in the closing couplet of ‘While My Lady Sleeps’ with its almost frenzied darts between the romantic and curiously exotic, and extended jazz-blues trip ‘Chronic Blues’.

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.

items.body:
Weirder, wider, knottier and more hypnotic than its predecessors, L'rain's fourth album closes out her opening act with a vivid firework display of canny cultural references, considered observations and, most crucially, heartbreakingly beautiful songs. It's dumbfounding material, the kind of omnivorous, masterful gear that just doesn't come around often enough - a future classic, to put it bluntly, FFO keiyaA, Mabe Fratti, Dawuna, Dijon or even Broadcast.

There's an aura of comprehensiveness that surrounds 'fata morgana'. Taja Cheek has fully broken in her influences and inspirations at this stage and works without hesitation, painting out her experiences of a broken world with a level of insight that's so rare it's almost unparalleled. We already know that Cheek is a forensic listener; 2024's 'I Killed Your Dog' was a chunky "anti-break-up" album that met sorrow head-on with psych rock, indie, classic R&B and haunted folk references, while its predecessor projected Cheek's ambition, embedding shoegaze and ambient influences into a widescreen collage of avant-garde expressions. It wasn't fusion, exactly, it was Cheek's real-world experience - both as an artist and a high-profile curator - inked on thick, deluxe stock in illuminated letters. And the cycle that she began in 2017 with her tape saturated debut comes to a close with 'fata morgana'.

'I Killed Your Dog' was well aware of its lineage, recorded and produced with a level of detail that immediately put it alongside '70s avant-rock and R&B classics, so 'fata morgana' scratches away another layer, making deeper, odder connections. Even the brief 'rumors of light' is anything but throwaway, casually introducing Cheek's voice through a hailstorm of looped interference that's broken up by disarming bouts of silence. This doesn't only slickly establish the record's experimental credentials, it echoes the eerie 'Transmission' tracks on DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing'. "This is not a dream," a garbled voice memorably stated, and Cheek's utterances hint at the exact opposite, a choppy mess of backmasked syllables, coughs and hesitations that suggest we're being lowered into a surreal fantasy. Fairytale muted piano phrases appear in the distance and 'with time' materializes on the horizon, kinked by buzzing oscillations that blur time just slightly until Cheek's whisper-sung vocals sidestep into the candlelight. 

Already, it's Cheek's most enigmatic track, occupying the confounding spot between an acid-tweaked Laurel Canyon memory, a half-heard gospel standard and Wendy Carlos's iconic 'The Shining' score: beautiful, meaningful and effortlessly cinematic. And Cheek continues to paint outside the lines, concocting half-song 'blue' from tape-mangled brass loops and gunky drum improvisations that she scrapes into a seductive, hazed atmosphere underneath her reverberating chorals. It's tempting to reference shoegaze or dream pop; the end result is similar, texturally at least, but 'fata morgana' is comprised of hardier raw material: minerals crushed by hand from funk, spiritual jazz, reggae, blues and rock 'n roll. That's never more obvious than on the gorgeous 'july 5th', when smudged folk - mixed with screaming feedback and analog bleeps, of course - mutates into a jerky soundsystem banger in its final act, imagining what OutKast's 'B.O.B.' might sound like if Atlanta was swapped out for Kingston.

Then there's the brassy standout 'elmyra', an anthemic start-stop post-pop banger that's part 'Haha Sound'-era Broadcast and part Wire, distorted to a level that would terrify most green-gilled pretenders. All this, and we haven't even mentioned the album's dense, maximalist lead single 'Soulless Cycle', a track that begins with chattering, bit-crushed samples and double-time kicks and lunges towards its glittering, psychedelic wall of sound that stands as an apt metaphor for the melancholy cacophony of contemporary reality. Before the album's done, Cheek slides in a lysergic slow jam ('birthday') and a near-ambient darkjazz diversion ('church of no one'), reminding us that perseverance and resilience is still possible - preferable, in fact.

Seriously, it's one of those albums that reminds you why you started caring about music in the first place, a milestone that's both cognizant of its place in history and hyper aware of the current moment. So, so good.

items.body:
Lower case, gently effervescent electronica from the softer underbelly of the US scene, turning extramusical cues from the collected writings of Julian of Norwich - the earliest writing of any woman in English.

“On revelations of divine love, jason calhoun’s fifth release for Dear Life Records, Calhoun has assembled an especially potent album of work that whirrs, hums, and glows. Unlike his recent output centered around extended, hypnotic compositions, the fourteen tracks here immediately request your attention and curiosity. Their concision only underscores one of his greatest strengths: the ability to capture an evaporating, fleeting moment, and hold it close.

The title is a nod to British Anchoress Julian of Norwich, whose collected writing of the same title is the earliest of any woman written in English. Here it serves as a unifying theme for Calhoun's particular palette of restless textures and tentative melodies. This is personal music, to be sure, but it also feels tactile, almost taffy-like in its presentation—and with such a potent combination, it is hard to resist a smile while listening. Like when the insistent pulse grounding 'last one' suddenly changes color as yawning tones reveal themselves, or how 'eye dilation' tiptoes into the room with each note sounding like a carefully chosen step. Though never precious or fussy, the album remains resolutely intimate.

Calhoun puts it plainly: “Julian of Norwich says “‘All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well’. These days, I’ve been having my doubts that this is true. As no solution to the issue at hand, I look for the revelations of divine love in my life, and I find them--in my partner asleep on the floor in our studio, my survival of a social interaction with a stranger, being bad at chess. Don't ask me what they mean-I'm still figuring that out myself. Maybe we can figure it out together.” It is from this place of doubt, searching, and openness that the album finds its footing.

When asked about the origin of the album's cover art, Calhoun explained, "I see this spot all the time on my commute home from work". A true statement of how the mundane and meaningful are interwoven, from someone who celebrates that union better than most. Unlike Julian of Norwich, Calhoun is no hermetic mystic himself-but in his daily life he works at an oncology center, doing routine but necessary work to provide treatment for those in need of it. While he might resist any analogizing, it is sincerely easy to say that Calhoun's body of work, which is only fortified by revelations of divine love, also offers care and company.”

items.body:
In the 15+ years that have elapsed since 'Loop Finding Jazz Records' first shuffled out of his ambrosially dusty speakers, Jan Jelinek's most famous album has acquired an almost mythical status. Originally released via Pole's defunct Scape imprint, it now finds new life via Jelinek's own Faitiche label, for a new generation to marvel at one of the finest examples of loop-based electronic music typical of the early noughties.

Taking what reads like a pretty austere set of ingredients, Jelinek's technique revolves around a trio of elements which consist of second long cuts of 1960's-70's jazz recordings, the loop-finding modulation wheel (do your homework!) and the Moiré effect; albeit rendered in the acoustic as opposed to the image and spectral domains.

If all this sounds a bit academic, be assured that on record it is anything but; as crumbling edifices of mealy rhythms slowly pulse into life and swirl around your head like snow storms clashing with a dust devil. Taking sediments of fathom deep static then skimming the best stuff from the top, Jelinek opens through the dampened echoes of 'Moiré (piano & organ)' wherein a slow-motion thrum of spiraling clicks, rustles and analogue tones conspire to give the impression of recondite perspectives that extend well beyond the constituent elements.

Elsewhere, 'Rocky in the Video Age' instills a gratuitously optimistic blush to the aquatic micro-sound ebb, 'Moiré (Strings)' is a perfect companion to Basinski's disintegrating tape archive, whilst 'Them, Their' represents an aural crease so sleight you can only catch its distinctive gleam from the corner of your eye.

items.body:
First full collaborative LP from Open Mike Eagle & Kenny Segal after nearly twenty years of friendship and occasional collaboration.

"It’s five years in a blender. It’s every troublesome misunderstanding of a half-decade relationship distorted and stretched into an absurdist black comedy mini-series on wax. It’s the sound of every fight we ever had, playing simultaneously. It’s several consecutive voice notes that you did not listen to, and instead read the transcription. It’s fifteen songs from iconoclastic rapper Mike Eagle and innovative producer Kenny Segal. It’s the world’s first half-whimsical break-up album. It’s DOOMED!

It’s also LA. Maybe not first and foremost, but Los Angeles runs deep in this record’s present, and its lineage. The story of any big city is also one of transplants. DJ Premier in New York, Tupac in California. If you build it, they will come. Mike and Kenny both arrived in LA as young, aspiring artists who were drawn to the scene around groundbreaking rap crew Project Blowed. They have been friends—and occasional collaborators—for almost twenty years. Despite that, DOOMED! is the first time the two have put together a full body of work. But everything happens in its time, and fate worked to bring them together at the exact moment that would allow the duo to create something extraordinary. Mike, fresh off a string of multi-producer records and processing the end of a tumultuous relationship, was in need of creative catharsis.

Meanwhile, Kenny had locked in on his next challenge after a recent string of critically acclaimed collaborations not only with rappers like billy woods, and K-the-I???, but also jazz trio Human Error Club and bluesy indie rocker Benjamin Booker.

“In recent years, Kenny made it very clear that he wasn’t trying to keep having one or two beats on my projects; he wanted to build something,” Open Mike Eagle explains. “I was able to convince him to let me use a couple beats for Neighborhood Gods Unlimited with the caveat that we would focus on our thing next. Then my relationship fell apart right when we started working, and it was like, ‘Perfect, I have a lot to say about this.’

Here are some more particularly interesting insights from the man himself:

“If DOOMED! is prestige TV, then think of “Out To Lunch” as the pilot where we meet a man who’s not all there because his head is still in yesterday, and the following as a brief synopsis. There’s a song that starts at an argument about the color of a rental car. There’s a song about trying to write a pair of lovers’ initials in wet concrete and the stick breaking. There’s a song that’s a prayer about finding the strength not to look at my ex’s social media. There’s a song about a character from Adventure Time who’s a piece of shit that I identify with. Each vision is a crashed airplane halfway on the border of dream and nightmare, bitter and sweet, sadness and freedom. Every one of Kenny’s beats is a chunk of ore from a different comet. I used each one as a canvas to paint my impression of a dead world.""

items.body:
Dalhous's first demo collection, originally released on Blackest Ever Black back in 2015. RIYL Ekoplekz, Christ or Forest Swords.

Officially established by Edinburgh-based duo Marc Dall and Alex Ander in 2012, the name Dalhous was really just a formality - the duo had already been working on material together, under the name Young Hunting, for years. This is the era that's properly dredged up here, compiling the demos that Ander and Dall originally compiled for an Intergalactic FM broadcast, eventually dubbing it to tape to fill a gap after the release of 'Will to be Well'. And it's good material, especially if you're interested in tracking the project's evolution. Picking up where that other notorious Scottish electronic duo left off when they wrote 'Twoism', Ander and Dall are fascinated by the kind of moods that disappeared when VHS was traded up for DVD. Not completely in thrall to B-movie soundtracks and documentary themes, Dalhous prefer to muddle their sound with rusted industrial grot, amping up the distortion and making sure the beats fall neatly off the grid. At 21 tracks, it's a lot to plow through, but it's tidy listening if you've already exhausted the duo's proper albums.

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s hugely influential debut LP of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smoked out nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueur, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state.  So strong was the impact of the album on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

Proper, tracky, Chi-style budgers from the badboy Delroy Edwards, back to his vintage tricks on spiritual home L.A. Club Resource

The jakbeat is strong on this one, laid down direct and cruddy in the best sense with drum machines and  synths toiled into driving grooves that sound like they could have emerged during the mid ‘80s early years of house. Covering the spectrum of jakbeat flavours, he crosses from the title tune’s sultry swerve to hypnotic bass goop in ‘Put That’, cruising from the rude Adonis like keys of ‘Bring The House’ to a smart glimmer of FM synthesis smeared into ‘How’d You Do That’, and some Faces drums-style machine tickets on ‘Don’t Ya Know’, saving the punchiest tackle for the percolated funk and honk of ’Sweet Geese’, and dope nods to Gene Hunt on ‘House Blitz.’

items.body:
All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.

items.body:
Moving sideways from Warp to Domino, Simian Mobile Disco's James Ellis Ford challenges himself on his second solo full-length, crafting a set of Sakamoto-inspired synth pop from his hospital bed.

Ford's always been capable of producing pitch-perfect pop - his appearance on records from everyone from the Pet Shop Boys to Depeche Mode is a testament to that - but 'Lost in Another World' is a more personal affair. It was written and produced in hospital after he'd been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia last year, "on the ward between rounds of chemo." Thankfully his condition has improved - he posted earlier this month that he's got no more treatment in store - but the album stands as a vulnerable reflection of a difficult time. Ford describes it as a "pep talk", and it draws on some of his most enduring influences, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Japan, to channel its complicated tangle of emotions. 

On the opening track (and lead single) 'Overtones', Ford's voice hovers over plasticky rhythmelodic sequences and rubbery '80s drums and you'd be forgiven for assuming it's a lost city pop demo. Ford doesn't let the energy fall off, either, waltzing through slow-motion melancholia on the tentatively beautiful 'Here Today' and John Foxx-style synth pop on 'This Too Shall Pass'. Ultimately, it's surprisingly hopeful material, infused with genuine feeling.

Hair-kissing house shuffle, ambient-breaks, and offbeat electro, from a regular of Nous'klaer Audio and Studio Barnhus, returning to Tokyo’s Mule Musiq.

Effortlessly poised for festival waft-offs, the ‘Ever Changing EP’ cycles thru the night from a kinked kind of cumbia house shuffle stroked with lush subs and layered with angel breath pads in ‘Through You’, to ambient breaks nodding to early AFX on ‘Unfold’, while tucking away a romantic, harmonised house slug in ‘Multitudes’, and snapping to dusted electro-breaks on the moodier closer, ‘Continuum’.

items.body:
Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.

Recorded last year, 'Lynboril Linsinopril' is a lengthy session from seasoned improvisers Adam Bohmen (on strings and amplified objects), Sue Lynch (on woodwind) and Crystabel Efemena Riley (on percussion).

All members of London's Horse Improvised Music Club, Bohmen, Lynch and Riley are motivated by the act of playing, something that's evident immediately. There's a refreshing freedom to their approach; it's relatively straightforward free improv gear, with Riley's tuff rhythm section providing an anchor for her collaborators' wildest skronk-y expressions, but breathes outside of the usual boundaries, never falling into the expected locked grooves. If you follow Cafe Oto's orbiting improv scene, this'll be worth a closer look.

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.

items.body:
Scoring a graphic novel based on a dream he had in 2024, John Carpenter gets the band back together, turning in an album that'll delight fans of 'Lost Themes'.

We know full well that Hollywood doesn't seem interested in making Carpenter's films a reality any more - he's said as much, quite publicly. So what's the next best thing? Well, a graphic novel. 'Cathedral' was written by Carpenter alongside his wife (and long-time creative partner) Sandy King and, like all great Carpenter projects, it had to have a home-brewed score to ease it along. So who better to make the dream a reality than his regular bandmates Cody Carpenter and Daniel Davies? Chronologically, this one fits in right after 2024's 'Lost Themes No. 4: Noir', but fans of Carpenter's earlier (eerier) biz will be happy to hear that he's reaching a little further back this time. 

There's of course the hard rock influence that's been present since at least 'They Live', but every so often there's a glimmer of the earworm-laden synth pop that elevated 'Escape from New York', and the iconic 'Assault on Precinct 13'. Just peep the 'Halloween'-style piano breakdown on 'Inside Out', the 'In the Mouth of Madness' mood on opener 'Primeval' or the classic horror flex of 'Abandoned Cathedral', with its organs, orchestral swells and all-important Mellotron choirs.

items.body:
Munich’s modern art gallery Museum Brandhorst field wide ranging responses to an exhibit of works and concerts focussed on the works of John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg and Cy Twombly, ranging from the sound poetry of Sofia Biazzi; to the sublime levitations of Maria Margolina; avant ambient pop of water lily; the pulsating technoid attack of focus baby; andCaroline Kretschmer’s subaquatic intrigue.

“Museum Brandhorst has invited Sound and Experiment to create a series of performances, audio works, and concerts in relation to the exhibition Fünf Freunde: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly. The event took place on June 27, 2025, as part of the Junge Nacht and the opening night of the annual Kunstareal Fest in Munich. The program featured newly produced pieces by Sound and Experiment participants Sofian Biazzi, Ilinca Fechete, focus baby, Daniel Gianfranceschi, Bruno Haas, Caroline Kretschmer, Bradley Leonard, Camilla Metelka, Maria Margolina, rosi and water lily. 

In a preparatory, biweekly seminar, discussions addressed conditions such as spectrotemporal displays, sharing time and frequency domains with different sound pieces simultaneously, and eventual performance constellations. An additional point of departure was a close reading of the indirect role of American artist David Tudor in some of the positions exhibited in Fünf Freunde, the function of the organization E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), and auditory scene analysis and synthesis in general.

The pieces featured on this CD are related to the presented performances, yet newly produced and with the audio CD format in mind.”

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.

items.body:
Thee darkest, weirdest dub perennial from Keith Hudson, 1979, blooms on vinyl for first time in years, ready to scatter smoke and minds into the late and early hours...

First released in 1979 and highly in-demand ever since, the dub sibling to Keith Hudson’s ‘Nuh Skin Up’ pushes that album’s already stark blooz and The Soul Syndicate’s deadly riddims hard into the echo chamber with a balance of experimental nous and heads-down grooves that has assured its place in the pantheon of the most haunting dubs. 

Out of print for decades until a 2007 pressing spiked it back in the water table, the album firmly holds up nearly a half century since its original release on the basis of a future proofed minimalism that continues to haunt successive generations with its bony percussion and a dematerialised soul exemplary of dub metaphysics at its transcendant best.

Up there with the likes of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry in terms of his dual role as songwriter and desk-tweaking dub maverick, Hudson really gets inside his own tunes, and The Soul Syndicate’s instrumentals, with the uncanniest insight, turning the likes of its title corker into clouds of pillowy steppers bass and streaking echoic contrails.

The way he inverts the vocals on ‘Ire Ire’ to sound properly wrong-end-of-telescope against the foregrounded crack of congas and spectral organ is just magic, and lays the groundwork for so much dub experimentation to come from the likes of everyone from Rhythm & Sound to Tricky, along with the likes of his spellbinding, skeletal steppers dub masterwork ‘Troubles’.

items.body:
Mu-inspired space cadets KiF Productions livicate their play of Japanese environmental ambient electronics, Hassellian 4th world, the KLF’s ‘Chill Out’, and Eno-esque harmonic perfumes, to the dearly departed Keith McIvor​.

"Passiflora (Passifloraceae) is a genus of around 550 species of flowering plants, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. The Passion Flower is a plant of improbable beauty - its blooms almost too intricate to be real, its climbing habit a quiet kind of determination. It has been used for centuries as a remedy for anxiety and sleeplessness, something that slows us and the world around us down.

Fresh from last year's triumphant debut by KiF; Still Out, Passiflora, the album, follows the plant from its very beginning. It opens in darkness - 'Secret of the Seed', dormant, waiting - before the first tentative stir of 'First Movement' and the long, instinctive reach of 'Seeking Light'. From there, the journey unfolds with the patience of something that has no choice but to grow: drinking, climbing, flowering. 'Song of the Vine' carries the plant's quiet insistence upward, while 'Florescence' and 'Pollination Dream' catch it at its most open - that brief, extraordinary moment of full bloom. Then the turn. 'Fruiting (Slight Return)' and finally 'Return to Earth' - the cycle completing itself, giving back what it always borrowed.

Each track is a stage. The whole is a life cycle."

items.body:
Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees.

‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with a local farmer on how “birds are the architects of the living landscape”. It follows some 40 solo albums over the past 20 years (not to mention jams with Woven Skull and Tomuttontu) with a considered approach to what lies just beyond her home; typically drawing on her attentive reading of the rural soundsphere to transmute the poetry of birdsong and the natural world into expressive musical metaphor.

The low bowed cello tone of regular spar Eimear Reidy underlines and opens out a breezy space where where the fiddle and violinists criss-cross air in reserved melodic flight and plucky figures that alternate like the play of light on Ireland’s remote North West. The piece unfolds to boggy pockets of percussion and passages of barely-there, hushed gloam, as though the wind itself was generating the players’ gestures, which rise to cloud castle hover around the midway, only to depart for Nyahh label boss Willie Stewart’s rolling drum thunder and scrape of Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh's fiddle rooted in the rolling landscape. Ultimately the folk soul of the turf rises in its final section, resembling a rousing, swaying folk song voiced by the strings in ideally creaky discord.

items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."

Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.

items.body:
Cloud-seeding dub techno sorcery x Rhythm & Sound worship by Stephen Hitchell’s cult cv313 and Radius projects, recorded in the heart of Detroit and preserved for posterity by Pole’s faithful remasters at Scape Berlin.

Echospace co-pilot Stephen Hitchell mans the cockpit solo on six sterling examples of Motor City dub techno purism within the 1st volume of ‘Altering Illusions’. His hallucinatory, synaesthetic tekkerz are in palpable effect from the damp bass thru to its noctilucent synth haze, bathing bodies in blissed-out arrangements that unfold up to 20 minutes in length, as with the echoes of BC’s ‘radiance’ registered in expansive parting piece ‘standing still’, and dredged up from drizzly depths on the cv313 rewire of Radius’ ‘Interpolation Tapes’.

Clubs are in the rearview for an 80 min trip deep under the hood of Echospace’s classic sound, fathoming deepest levels of sunken subs and elemental attrition on ‘i s i s’, and hingeing on Rhythm & Sound’s skankers' templates in ‘hypnosphere’ and mesmerising metallic resonance of ‘irradiate’, while ‘above clouds’ rises above the weather system into clearer, blue-skied dub techno lushness; think post-storm Lake Erie panoramas diffused by Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS.

items.body:
Derek Bailey, Loren Connors and Bill Orcutt fiends will be in their element with Nathan Roche’s 2nd salvo of experimental twangers for a resurrected Celluloid; the legendary label with roots in post-punk & NYC mutations, who would also  issue ‘The Lambada’ - the biggest selling global single of ’89.

Hailing to France, via Townsville, North east Queensland, and Sydney, Australia, Nathan Roche has carved out an uncompromising catalogue of guitar abstractions since the ‘00s with myriad outfits, including turns on Siltbreeze, London’s World of Echo, and France’s excellently titled Gone With The Weed label.

After helping reboot the Celluloid label with his very psych-garage-rock LP ’35 Rue du Théâtre’ in 2025, the dozen succinct bits of ‘aa in reverse’ mark a sharp departure from the classic composure of his previous works, and into fractious deconstructions of blues guitar vernacular, very much in the vein of iconoclasts, Derek Bailey, Bill Orcutt, or Tetuzi Akiyama, but accented with his own twang.

In this abstract blues mode Nqthqn reserves the right to really jangle and pluck the listener’s nerves in tart, prickly expressions that favour microtonality and dissonance over more consonant, Western pleasures. The warp and weft of his material snags from the off with the distended notes of ‘astra’ thru the rudely detuned mix elegance and grunt in ‘aa’, pulling into Loren Connors-esue midnight melancholy on ‘aka’ and relatively stretching out into 3 mins of curdled to finely melodic chops on ‘adversary’.

items.body:
Death Is Not The End return to the soul-stir sound of deep south Sacred Harp Singers in 1993 - although it could feasibly be any time since the advent of portable tape recording - in the blessed company of the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark, Alabama. Feels just right in this humidity…

The Wiregrass Singers' Dewey Williams began learning the shape-note tradition in his childhood. He studied under Judge Jackson, who authored the landmark 1934 hymnbook The Colored Sacred Harp. In 1971, Williams formally organized The Wiregrass Sacred Harp Singers to preserve the music full-time. This unified troupe began touring nationally and leading workshops, which ultimately launched them onto stages at the Smithsonian and Newport folk festivals up until Williams' passing in 1995 when the group disbanded. The African-American Sacred Harp tradition in the Wiregrass region has steeply declined since the start of the 21st century, due to an aging generation of singers, and today it is largely sustained through archival preservation and occasional multi-book singing meetups.

This raw recording, made at the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark in mid-April 1993 finds the group singing from B. F. White’s The Sacred Harp (1844), which together with his brother-in-law William Walker’s Southern Harmony (1835) formed the musical backbone of generations of Southern music and Southern musical styles.

items.body:
Colin Stetson’s breakthrough album of gripping bass sax innovations still buzzes like few others.

In 2007 ‘New History Warfare Vol.1’ asserted Stetson as an indomitable player of wind instruments, here letting off on Alto, Baritone and Bass Saxophones, plus Clarinet, in a deftly muscular display of his skills which had previously been employed on record and in live tours for Arcade Fire, Tom Waits, Bon Iver, LCD Soundsystem and whoever the heck else needed a set of lungs as good as a blacksmith’s bellows.

While perhaps best known for wielding a massive Bass Saxophone that's responsible for some of the wildest sounds on this album, Stetson proves to be a sensitive beast capable of articulating the instrument’s full range tonal in his own voice, which variously comes out resembling a purring big cat and the dying wildebeest it just stalked, attacked and slaughtered in ‘Time Is Advancing With Fitful Irregularity’, while he uses the same broad tone to describe natural scenes as textured with soil and moisture and wind as an Anne Guthrie piece in ‘As a Bird or Branch’, while ‘Nobu Take’ sounds like a manic 8-bit computer game soundtrack and ’Tiger Tiger Crane’ adds a tight percussive workout for good measure, but trust its all acoustic, instrumental, hands-on, somehow not processed. 

Still a stonking good record, this, ripe for re/discovery.

items.body:
All killer, no filler trotters from a golden period of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s foundational work at fabled studio, The Black Ark.

This 3rd in a prized series spies the wee madman conjuring multidimensional spectres from vocal recordings of regular spars: Max Romeo, The Jolly Brothers, Leroy Sibbles, The Mistic, and Devon Irons. Perry’s visionary, innovative application of studio-as-instrument tekkerz come to the fore in the music’s layered diffusions, which we may take for granted in contemporary music, but was radical back then, and whose uncanny appeal has only steeped with age. 

Including a solo standout in the ghostly, harmonised roots wooze of his ‘Dread Lion’ gem as King Scratch, it spans the signature, lysergic sparkle of his ‘Conscious Man’cut with The Jolly Brothers, thru a stepping 12” mix of Max Romeo’s ‘Norman’ (1978), and heat-hazed sway to Leroy Sibbles’ ‘Garden of Life’, along with The Mistic’s eyes-down devotional ‘Forward With Jah’, and sloshing nyabingi of ‘When Jah Comes’ for Devon Irons.

items.body:
Techgnostic pied piper of Latin club, Tra Tra Trax co-founder Verraco hustles a class handful of techno, electro and hard groove bustlers for German compilation series The Third Room.

The Colombian producer-DJ takes The Third Room’s brief, to create a “place where different cultures existing and correlating to each other, mix and transform into hybrids” his own way, after precedents laid by Oscar Mulero, Freddy K, and GiGi FM, among others.

An exclusive ’Stone Version’ of Substance & Vainqueur’s 2007 dub techno ace ‘Libration’ opens a set spanning Skee Mask’s frisky deep techno swanger ‘Clear Sky 909’, thru the shearing sound design of Verraco’s own ‘Untitled (Teamgeist Mix)’, to the polyrhythmic hard groove charge of LA’s 1morning, and compatible tackle of ‘PatumPa’ by Monterrey, Mexico’s Regal86.

items.body:
An ATL house and soul don hustles in-the-pocket bossa, broken beat, and deep boogie grooves, bolstered with Ben Hixon’s dubby Salsoul-style remix.

Marquinn Mason’s vocals elevate the session to classiest lounge club levels, dusting a jazz-soul flow to the Brazilian shuffle of ‘Bossa Beat’, and oiling the broken beat angularity of ‘Bounce’, before ideally adapting to the squashed electro-soul boogie of ‘Moving Steady’, and reminding of Omar-S joints with John F.M. ben Hixon’s remix only accentuates that comparison with a supple ATL-via-313-and-NYC Salsoul deep house appeal.
